( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa.** When there is an extremely intense craving for eating meat, he states that the desire should be diverted in this way, rather than justifying the slaughter of animals. He says, "One should make," meaning one should prepare an animal made of clarified butter <note>a symbolic offering</note> because it is similar to animal flesh, and in the same way, an animal made of flour. "In a state of craving" <term>saṅge</term> means extreme desire. Some say <term>saṅge</term> refers to the oppression by elemental spirits, but as this is not widely known in the world, the former reason holds. 37.

( 3 ) **Kullūka.** <term>Saṅge</term> means in a state of attachment. Due to a craving for eating meat, one should make an image of an animal out of clarified butter or flour and consume that. One should never desire to kill animals without having a specific deity in mind. 37.

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda.** "Animal of clarified butter" means an animal image made of clarified butter. "In a state of craving" refers to being addicted to animal sacrifice or having a strong craving for eating meat during necessary rituals or traditional domestic duties. This does not apply to Vedic rituals where, for instance, a real goat must be sacrificed to satisfy the eleven sacrificial posts. Therefore, it is said that slaughter in a sacrifice is not considered slaughter. 37.

( 5 ) **Nandana.** He says, "One should make," to indicate that one should not perform slaughter contrary to the prescribed method. "In a state of craving" <term>saṅge</term> refers to occasions like festivals when relatives gather. One should consecrate an animal of clarified butter <note>a substitute offering</note>. This means that instead of a real animal, one should offer abundant clarified butter, flour, or cakes. 37.

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra.** One should make an animal of clarified butter when there is a craving. One should do the same with an animal of flour. One should never desire to kill an animal in vain. 37.

### For as many hairs as the animal has, so many times in birth after birth, the one who kills an animal in vain shall suffer slaughter in the next world. 38

( 1 ) **Medhātithi.** He shall suffer as many deaths as there are hairs <note>on the animal</note> in future births. "The one who kills an animal in vain" is one who performs animal slaughter not commanded by Vedic or Smṛti texts. Such slaughter is often performed by hunters and others for worldly purposes. The word <term>paśughna</term> <gloss>animal-killer</gloss> is a Vedic grammatical form. 38.

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa.** "So many times" means an equal number of times. "The one who kills an animal in vain" refers to one who kills an animal without the sanction of the Vedas or Smṛtis. 38.

( 3 ) **Kullūka.** One who kills animals for their own pleasure without the intent of offering to a deity is a killer of animals in vain. After death, in birth after birth, he suffers slaughter as many times as there are hairs on the animal. Therefore, one should not kill animals in vain. The particle <term>ha</term> here is used to indicate established scriptural tradition. 38.

( 4 ) **Rāghavānanda.** He states a punishment for the opposite case by saying, "For as many..." The particle <term>ha</term> here signifies something well-known. 38.

( 5 ) **Nandana.** "So many times" means that many occasions. The particle <term>ha</term> is used to express compassion. 38.

( 6 ) **Rāmacandra.** A person who kills an animal in vain, having committed the sin of slaughter in this world, attains the form of an animal in birth after birth as many times as there are hairs on the animal, specifically eighty million hairs. 38.

### Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice. Sacrifice is for the prosperity of all; therefore, slaughter in a sacrifice is not slaughter. 39

( 1 ) **Medhātithi.** This does not incur the fault mentioned previously. The slaughter is for the sake of the sacrifice, which is commanded by the Veda and Smṛti, and is for the sake of that prosperity which is the removal of <note>ritual</note> impurity. The "Self-Existent One" <term>Svayambhū</term>, meaning Prajāpati, created or produced animals. "Himself" is an <term>arthavāda</term> <gloss>eulogistic statement</gloss>. The "sacrifice" <term>yajña</term>, such as the Jyotiṣṭoma, is for the entire world. "Prosperity" <term>bhūtyai</term> means wealth, nourishment, and growth. Therefore, the slaughter there is to be understood as "non-slaughter." It is said this way because of the removal of the sin that would otherwise be caused by violence. 39.

( 2 ) **Sarvajña Nārāyaṇa.** Here, he clears up the doubt regarding how there can be an absence of such a fault when killing for the sake of sacrifice. He says, "For the sake of sacrifice." The prosperity of the world comes from the cycle of offerings that nourish the sun, causing rain, which creates seeds, which leads to the production of vital energy and the birth of living beings. By this, it is stated that because many beings are sustained through the sacrifice of one animal, there is an absence of that specific fault. 39.

<summary>This page explains that ritual animal sacrifice is not considered sinful because it serves the greater prosperity of the world and is divinely sanctioned, unlike the killing of animals for personal pleasure, which results in karmic retribution.</summary>
<keywords>animal sacrifice, ritual, non-violence, karma, rebirth, Medhātithi, Kullūka, Yajña, Svayambhū</keywords>
